spine: 1. Async replica reads break read-your-writes because commit visibility on the primary is not the same event as replay completion on the standby — the app has no channel to ask the replica where it stands, so it guesses with timeouts or flags.

2. Replica lag is three separable waits, not one number: write_lag and flush_lag are network/disk mechanics; replay_lag is the bottleneck because recovery is a single sequential process, and a conflicting standby query can block replay for up to max_standby_streaming_delay (30s default) before being cancelled.

3. Naive replica reads miss the just-committed write extremely often (99.2% even on a same-machine loopback replica in boringsql's test) — and offloading more reads to the replica makes replay compete harder for resources, worsening the exact lag being avoided.

4. PostgreSQL 19 (tested against postgres:19beta3) adds WAIT FOR LSN: a client captures pg_current_wal_flush_lsn() on the primary AFTER commit, then issues WAIT FOR LSN '<lsn>' WITH (MODE 'standby_replay', TIMEOUT '...', NO_THROW) on the replica before reading — the replica only serves the read if it has actually replayed up to that LSN.

5. TIMEOUT does not control correctness — in boringsql's benchmark, stale reads stayed at 0/400 whether TIMEOUT was 20ms (all reads fell back to primary, p50 24.0ms) or 500ms (all served by replica, p50 53.4ms) against a fixed 50ms replica lag. TIMEOUT only decides which node serves the read and how long it waits, and a cluster-wide lag event can time out every waiter simultaneously and stampede the primary.

6. The three alternatives shift cost differently: reading the primary always gives up replica offload entirely; a fixed sleep/sticky window pays the same latency regardless of whether the replica actually needed it; synchronous_commit=remote_apply makes every writer (not just the reader who needs freshness) pay a replay-wait on every commit.

7. The mechanism has hard scope limits: it only covers the specific writes whose LSNs the caller is holding, cannot run inside a function/procedure/DO block or above READ COMMITTED isolation, and a load-balanced pooler endpoint can route the WAIT and the subsequent read to two different replicas, silently breaking the guarantee.

perspective.mechanism: Replica lag decomposes into write_lag/flush_lag (network+disk) and replay_lag (single sequential WAL-apply process on the standby); PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN lets a client capture its post-commit write LSN on the primary and block on the replica, in MODE standby_replay with a TIMEOUT, until that LSN has actually been replayed and is query-visible, rather than polling pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() itself.
perspective.tradeoff: TIMEOUT trades off which node serves a read and how long the caller waits, not correctness (stale reads stay at zero on both sides of the threshold in their benchmark) — but a short TIMEOUT under a cluster-wide lag spike can synchronize a stampede back to the primary, and a waiting reader holds a pool connection for the full wait, so the budget has to be sized against pool capacity.
perspective.reader_use: A Taiwanese backend engineer shipping read-replica offload today would use this to replace ad-hoc sleep-then-read or sticky-to-primary windows with a bounded, per-request wait that only pays cost when a read genuinely needs the just-written row — while budgeting for PgBouncer/load-balancer routing constraints, the READ COMMITTED-only restriction, and ORM write-detection false positives (Rails Active Record) before adopting it.

perspective.mechanism: Official reference for pg_current_wal_lsn(), pg_current_wal_flush_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), and pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() — their return type (pg_lsn) and exact semantics (write vs flush vs replay position; NULL when not in recovery).
perspective.tradeoff: These functions are the pre-existing, poll-based way to answer 'has the replica caught up' — functionally correct but requires the client to loop and compare LSNs itself, racing across two separate connections.
perspective.reader_use: Grounds the 'crude polling' baseline this post contrasts WAIT FOR LSN against, and confirms the exact function names/signatures used in the post are real Postgres APIs rather than paraphrase.

perspective.mechanism: synchronous_commit's remote_apply value makes a commit on the primary wait until the synchronous standby has received AND applied (replayed) the commit record, so it is visible to queries there — a stronger, more expensive guarantee than the default 'on'.
perspective.tradeoff: remote_apply closes the read-your-writes gap for every reader by making every writer pay a replay-wait on every commit, regardless of whether any reader will need that freshness soon.
perspective.reader_use: Lets a reader independently verify boringsql's framing that remote_apply is the 'write pays for everyone' alternative to WAIT FOR LSN's 'only the reader who needs it pays'.

perspective.mechanism: max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30s) is the time a standby waits before cancelling a standby query that conflicts with about-to-be-applied WAL, when WAL is arriving via streaming replication; synchronous_standby_names lists which standbys are eligible to participate in synchronous replication.
perspective.tradeoff: A longer max_standby_streaming_delay protects long-running standby queries at the cost of letting replay (and therefore read-your-writes freshness) fall further behind.
perspective.reader_use: Confirms the exact default value (30s) the post cites for the mechanism that can block WAL replay behind a conflicting long query, and clarifies the division of labor between synchronous_standby_names (eligibility) and synchronous_commit (how far to wait) referenced in the post's remote_apply discussion.

perspective.mechanism: Canonical distributed-systems definition: read-your-writes (read-my-writes) requires that a process's own subsequent read observes the effects of its own prior write; it explicitly does not constrain what a process sees of writes performed by other processes.
perspective.tradeoff: Because the guarantee's scope is deliberately narrow (own writes only), any single mechanism that satisfies it (like WAIT FOR LSN) is not automatically a general staleness fix for reads of other people's writes.
perspective.reader_use: Gives the post's 'idea' section a rigorous, source-backed name and scope for the everyday symptom described in the concrete-case section, and explains precisely why boringsql's closing caveat ('covers the writes whose LSNs you are holding and nothing else') is the correct scope, not an arbitrary limitation.

notes.quote: every change sent over a websocket invalidates state on every teammate's open tab and device, and all of them go back to the same endpoints on the same replicas.
notes.interpretation: Used as the concrete-case illustration of how collaborative/real-time products amplify the read-your-writes problem: many tabs re-read the same replica set at once, right after one of them wrote.

notes.quote: Your application has to act like a traffic conductor. It guesses the replication lag using timeouts and Redis flags. The replica already knows exactly where it stands; your code just has no way to ask. PostgreSQL 19 adds a way to ask.
notes.interpretation: The article's own framing of the 'before' state, used as the bridge from the concrete-case section into the LSN mechanism section.

notes.quote: write_lag and flush_lag are the mechanics of the network and the disk on the standby.
notes.interpretation: Definition used verbatim (translated context added) in the glossary tooltip widget.

notes.quote: replay_lag is the problem. Shipping WAL is usually simple; applying it is the part that makes your change visible to queries.
notes.interpretation: Identifies replay_lag as the bottleneck; used in the glossary tooltip and as the thesis of the 'three waits' section.

notes.quote: Recovery is a single startup process replaying records one at a time, and while prefetch can warm the I/O ahead of it, nothing applies two records at once.
notes.interpretation: Explains why replay_lag cannot be fixed by horizontal scaling; grounds the 4-layer pipeline widget and the 'why more replicas doesn't help L3' paragraph.

notes.quote: Replica waits up to max_standby_streaming_delay, 30 seconds by default, before killing the query blocking the replay.
notes.interpretation: Cited alongside the official docs (n17b) as the concrete number for how long a conflicting standby query can block replay before being cancelled.

notes.quote: this parameter determines how long the standby server should wait before canceling standby queries that conflict with about-to-be-applied WAL entries... If this value is specified without units, it is taken as milliseconds. The default is 30 seconds.
notes.interpretation: Official confirmation of the 30-second default for max_standby_streaming_delay cited by the article.

notes.quote: the more successfully you offload reads to the replica, the more lag you introduce there.
notes.interpretation: Used to explain why 'add more read replicas' can backfire on replay_lag specifically, since replay competes with the offloaded read queries for the same node's resources.

notes.quote: The replica is on the same machine as its primary and talks to it over loopback, and naive reads still miss 99.2% of the time.
notes.interpretation: The headline number for how unreliable naive replica reads are, used with an explicit inference (marked in prose) that a real cross-AZ network would likely not improve on this.

notes.quote: Read your writes (also known as read my writes) requires that if a process performs a write w, and that same process performs a subsequent read r, then r must observe w's effects.
notes.interpretation: Canonical definition of the consistency guarantee, used to formally name the everyday symptom from the concrete-case section.

notes.quote: Note that read your writes does not apply to operations performed by different processes.
notes.interpretation: Scope boundary of the guarantee; used to explain why the mechanism is deliberately narrow and does not solve general replica staleness for other readers.

notes.quote: WAIT FOR LSN '0/554D1B78' WITH (MODE 'mode', TIMEOUT 'timeout', NO_THROW)
notes.interpretation: Exact SQL syntax for the new PostgreSQL 19 statement, reproduced verbatim in the post's SQL code block.

notes.quote: MODE says what the standby has to have done with the WAL. standby_replay is the default and the only one that helps here: it waits until the record has been replayed and is visible to queries.
notes.interpretation: Explains the MODE parameter and confirms standby_replay is the only value the article documents in detail; the post explicitly notes it does not speculate about other MODE values.

notes.quote: // CaptureLSN runs on the PRIMARY, after the commit. Before it, or on any other connection, and you get a position that says nothing about your write. func CaptureLSN(ctx context.Context, primary *pgxpool.Pool) (string, error) { var lsn string; err := primary.QueryRow(ctx, "SELECT pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()::text").Scan(&lsn); return lsn, err }
notes.interpretation: Full Go function reproduced verbatim (reformatted for line length) as the post's worked-example code block.

notes.quote: Replayed asks one replica whether it has caught up to lsn, within budget. Any answer other than success (timeout, promotion, a dead replica) means "read the primary", so every failure path returns false rather than an error.
notes.interpretation: Comment-only description (no full code body available) of the wait function's failure semantics; used to explain NO_THROW's practical effect by inference, explicitly marked as inference in prose.

notes.quote: PoolFor is the whole routing decision: the replica has to earn the read.
notes.interpretation: Comment describing the routing function; used verbatim as the article's own summary phrase for the mechanism's core idea.

notes.quote: Don't compare them as strings. Cast to ::pg_lsn and let Postgres do the ordering.
notes.interpretation: Practical gotcha used in both the LSN-capture prose and the draggable LSN-catchup widget's figcaption.

notes.quote: pg_last_wal_replay_lsn () -> pg_lsn : Returns the last write-ahead log location that has been replayed during recovery. If recovery is still in progress this will increase monotonically. If recovery has completed then this will remain static at the location of the last WAL record applied during recovery. When the server has been started normally without recovery, the function returns NULL.
notes.interpretation: Official semantics for the three WAL/LSN functions named in the post (pg_current_wal_lsn, pg_current_wal_flush_lsn, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn), used to describe the pre-existing polling approach.

notes.quote: a cluster-wide lag event times out every waiter at roughly the same moment. The system then does the opposite of what you built it for and stampedes the primary with the traffic it was supposed to be shielded from.
notes.interpretation: Central risk of choosing too short a TIMEOUT; used verbatim in the cost/stampede paragraph.

notes.quote: a waiting reader holds a connection for the whole duration of the timeout.
notes.interpretation: Basis for the connection-pool budgeting point; the further consequence (pool exhaustion under simultaneous timeouts) is presented as the post's own extended reasoning, not a separate source claim.

notes.quote: recovery_min_apply_delay is known to delay commit records. This is the exact behaviour the pattern requires.
notes.interpretation: Explains how the article reproduced a controlled replica-lag scenario for its own testing.

notes.quote: All tests were run on postgres:19beta3, two containers on one host (Apple Silicon), a primary and one asynchronous streaming replica.
notes.interpretation: Test environment and version; used to flag PostgreSQL 19 as still in beta and the syntax as potentially subject to change before GA.

notes.quote: Read primary only | 0/1000 | 0 | 1.9ms | 3.1ms | 4.3ms || Read replica immediately | 992/1000 | 1000 | 1.8ms | 2.5ms | 9.2ms || Sleep 50ms, read replica | 0/1000 | 1000 | 53.9ms | 57.5ms | 62.0ms || WAIT FOR, read replica | 0/1000 | 1000 | 2.8ms | 4.2ms | 6.4ms
notes.interpretation: Baseline benchmark table (no added artificial lag, same-host replica) comparing the four read strategies; reproduced as the matter-of-fact-table widget.

notes.quote: TIMEOUT | stale reads | served by replica | fell back to primary | p50 :: 500ms | 0/400 | 400 | 0 | 53.4 ms :: 20ms | 0/400 | 0 | 400 | 24.0 ms
notes.interpretation: Benchmark with a fixed 50ms replica lag comparing two TIMEOUT settings; drives the interactive TIMEOUT-budget hero widget's step-function model (values below/at the 50ms lag threshold use these two measured anchors, not interpolated data).

notes.quote: When set to remote_apply, commits will wait until replies from the current synchronous standby(s) indicate they have received the commit record of the transaction and applied it, so that it has become visible to queries on the standby(s), and also written to durable storage on the standbys. This will cause much larger commit delays than previous settings since it waits for WAL replay.
notes.interpretation: Official semantics of synchronous_commit=remote_apply, used to explain the 'every writer pays' alternative.

notes.quote: Adding the standby to synchronous_standby_names took staleness from 593 out of 600 reads down to somewhere between 3 and 17, depending on the run.
notes.interpretation: The source itself reports a range with run-to-run variability rather than a single number; the post preserves this range rather than picking one value, and notes it as 'close but not fully closed'.

notes.quote: cannot be executed within a transaction with an isolation level higher than READ COMMITTED
notes.interpretation: Exact error-message-style constraint on WAIT FOR's usable isolation levels.

notes.quote: a snapshot held on a standby can block the replay that the wait is waiting for, at which point neither side moves.
notes.interpretation: Deadlock-shaped caveat; the post connects this explicitly to n26 as two faces of the same underlying issue (a held snapshot can block the very replay a wait depends on).

notes.quote: The pooler is the one component that already knows where each query is going, so it would be the natural place for this. But the wait and the read still have to reach the same node, so a pooler sitting in front of a load-balanced multi-replica endpoint breaks the pattern.
notes.interpretation: Explains why PgBouncer transaction-pooling works but a load-balanced multi-replica endpoint breaks the guarantee (WAIT and the subsequent read can land on different replicas).

notes.quote: Active Record decides whether a statement is a write by matching its leading keyword against an allowlist...WAIT FOR is not on that list, so it is a write by exclusion, and the reading role always prevents writes. The way through is to go under the statement layer, on the connection the read will use
notes.interpretation: Rails/Active Record integration caveat: WAIT FOR is misclassified as a write and blocked, requiring raw_connection access to issue it.

notes.quote: This is not a general fix for stale replicas. WAIT FOR covers the writes whose LSNs you are holding and nothing else.
notes.interpretation: The article's own scope boundary, echoing the Jepsen definition's 'own writes only' scope (n10); used for the post's closing caveat and the marked inference about readers who never wrote anything themselves.

notes.quote: it travels: a response header, a field on a job payload, a value you hand to another service ... It's a string like 0/3F8A120 identifying a WAL position and it isn't a secret.
notes.interpretation: Describes how the captured LSN string propagates through a request; used in the LSN-capture section and the closing paragraph.
